Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Substance use disorder (SUD) may contribute to tooth wear and temporomandibular disorders (TMDs), particularly in individuals undergoing opioid maintenance treatment (OMT). The primary aim of this study was to compare TMD-related clinical characteristics, including pain sensitivity, TMD presence, and tooth wear, between men in OMT and healthy controls. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This study included 37 males in OMT with a polysubstance use history and 37 controls. All participants underwent evaluation of pressure-pain thresholds (PPT), pain tolerance, and neck position sense. Presence of TMDs and tooth wear was evaluated by a maxillofacial surgeon. Severity of TMDs, posture, depression, and sleep quality were quantified using the Fonseca Anamnestic Index (FAI), New York Posture Rating Scale (NYPR), the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), respectively. RESULTS: Cervical proprioception differed significantly between groups (p < 0.001). Upper trapezius PPT and pain tolerance were lower in the OMT Group (p < 0.05). Tooth wear, TMD severity, sleep disturbance, and depression scores were higher, whereas posture scores were lower in the OMT group (p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: These findings support a comprehensive multidisciplinary assessment of oral, musculoskeletal, and psychosocial factors in individuals in OMT with a polysubstance use history.

item.title: Longitudinal Ultrasonographic Analysis of Involutional Changes after Radiofrequency Ablation of Papillary Thyroid Microcarcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Ham T, Lee JY, Lee M, Jeon YH, Hwang I, Rhim JH, Kim JH
item.description:
Authors: Ham T, Lee JY, Lee M, Jeon YH, Hwang I, Rhim JH, Kim JH
Journal: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association | DOI: 10.1177/10507256261494909
Published: 2026-Oct-07
PMID: 42844704



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) has emerged as an effective nonsurgical treatment for low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma (PTMC), with widely variable rates of complete disappearance reported. The purpose of our study was to characterize the longitudinal ultrasonographic (US) changes following RFA of PTMC and to propose imaging-based criteria to guide posttreatment surveillance. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 98 low-risk unifocal PTMC patients (82 females; age range, 27-59 years) who underwent RFA with a median follow-up of 48 months (range, 12-74 months). Comprehensive longitudinal US analysis was performed to characterize temporal changes in the ablation zone and surrounding parenchyma. Factors associated with postablational nodular remnant at 1 year after RFA were also evaluated. RESULTS: All RFA procedures achieved 100% technical success. By 1 year, the volume of the ablation zone had decreased to a median of 0 mL (range, 0-0.41 mL). However, ultrasonography demonstrated complete disappearance in only 70.4% of PTMCs, while 29.6% exhibited postablational nodular remnants despite volumetric resolution. These nodular remnants progressively regressed and eventually disappeared during subsequent follow-up, except for a single case of a tiny macrocalcified residue persisting at 5-year follow-up after RFA. Characteristic postablation US features gradually emerged during the first year after RFA, with incidence at 1 year of capsular retraction, postablational strands, and postablational parenchymal hypoechogenicity reaching 61.2%, 60.2%, and 51.0%, respectively. These findings remained relatively stable through the primary follow-up period of up to 36 months, although postablational strands showed a further significant increase in incidence throughout this period. Without major complications, disease progression occurred in 4.1% (4/98) patients: Three contralateral PTMC cases were treated with additional RFA, and one case with lymph node metastasis underwent surgery. No clinico-radiological or procedural factors were significantly associated with 1-year postablational nodular remnant after RFA. CONCLUSIONS: RFA of low-risk PTMC achieves an excellent final complete disappearance rate while frequently inducing characteristic US features, including capsular retraction, postablational strands, and postablational parenchymal hypoechogenicity. Recognition of these US involutional changes is crucial for accurate posttreatment monitoring and for avoiding misinterpretation of benign healing changes as pathological findings, and may inform imaging-based post-RFA surveillance.

item.title: Zingiberen Newsaponin Enhances Antitumor Immunity in Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma Via Induction of Autophagy-Dependent Pyroptosis.
item.dc:creator: Wang QX, Zou TX, Chen ZY, Wang XY, Li Q, Zhang JH, Cai YF, You J, Chen ED, Chen G, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Wang QX, Zou TX, Chen ZY, Wang XY, Li Q, Zhang JH, Cai YF, You J, Chen ED, Chen G, et al.
Journal: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association | DOI: 10.1177/10507256261493805
Published: 2026-Oct-07
PMID: 42844697



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is a lethal malignancy with a dismal prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Although immunotherapy has revolutionized the oncological landscape, the efficacy of Programmed Cell Death Protein 1 (PD-1) blockade as a monotherapy remains underwhelming in ATC. Consequently, identifying novel agents capable of triggering immunogenic cell death (ICD) to sensitize ATC to immune checkpoint inhibitors is a critical clinical priority. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Through high-throughput screening of 3200 compounds, Zingiberen newsaponin (ZN) was identified as a lead anti-ATC agent. Its therapeutic efficacy was evaluated using ATC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and xenograft models. Mechanistic investigations were conducted via pharmacological inhibition, genetic knockout, and Western blotting to examine the autophagy-pyroptosis axis. Furthermore, an immunocompetent murine ATC model was employed to assess the synergistic effects of ZN and anti-PD-1 therapy on the tumor immune microenvironment through immunohistochemical analysis of T-cell infiltration. RESULTS: ZN exhibited potent antiproliferative activity against ATC cells with half-maximal inhibitory concentration values ranging from 1.95 to 2.98 μM. Morphological assessment and biochemical assays (Lactate dehydrogenase, interleukin-1 beta, and high mobility group box 1 release) confirmed that ZN induces Gasdermin E (GSDME)-mediated pyroptosis via the activation of caspase-3 and caspase-8. Importantly, genetic knockout of GSDME significantly attenuated the pyroptotic phenotype, corroborating the central role of GSDME in ZN-induced pyroptosis. Mechanistically, ZN-induced pyroptosis was found to be autophagy-dependent, as pharmacological inhibition of autophagy with chloroquine significantly reversed GSDME cleavage and cell death both in vitro and in vivo. Consistently, ATG5 knockdown markedly rescued ZN-induced cell pyroptosis. Furthermore, ZN functioned as a potent inducer of ICD. In immunocompetent murine models, ZN treatment remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment by significantly increasing the infiltration of CD8+ T cells. Notably, the combination of ZN and anti-PD-1 therapy demonstrated superior synergistic antitumor efficacy compared with monotherapy. CONCLUSIONS: Our study identifies ZN as a novel inducer of autophagy-mediated GSDME pyroptosis in ATC. By triggering ICD and recruiting CD8+ T cells, ZN sensitizes ATC to PD-1 blockade, offering a promising therapeutic strategy for this lethal disease.

item.title: Comparative Performance of the 2015 and 2025 American Thyroid Association Initial Recurrence Risk Stratification Systems in Differentiated Thyroid Cancer.
item.dc:creator: Ke W, Zheng X, Wang L, Xiao Z, Chen W, Xu Y, Ke N, Huang P, Lin T, Shen Q, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Ke W, Zheng X, Wang L, Xiao Z, Chen W, Xu Y, Ke N, Huang P, Lin T, Shen Q, et al.
Journal: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association | DOI: 10.1177/10507256261494916
Published: 2026-Oct-07

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The 2025 American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines introduced significant modifications to the initial risk stratification system for differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC). However, the real-world prognostic performance and stage migration effects of these updates compared with the 2015 system remain unevaluated. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at a tertiary referral center in China. Adult patients who underwent initial thyroidectomy for pathologically confirmed DTC between January 2008 and December 2018 were included, with follow-up extending through October 30, 2025. We compared the 2015 and 2025 ATA initial risk stratification systems. The primary outcome was structural disease-free survival (SDFS). Performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), reclassification analysis, and decision curve analysis (DCA). RESULTS: Among 1508 patients (median age 43 years, interquartile range [IQR] = 33-53; 1147 [76.1%] female), 120 (8.0%) developed events during a median follow-up of 8.9 years (IQR = 7.56-10.80). The 2025 ATA system demonstrated superior discrimination compared with the 2015 system (ΔAUC 0.0455 [confidence interval or CI: 0.0147-0.0764], p = 0.004), although both systems showed significant risk stratification (log-rank p < 0.001). Reclassification analysis revealed that the 2025 system reassigned 41.7% of patients with recurrence to higher-risk categories but also reassigned 38.8% of recurrence-free patients to higher-risk categories. Multivariable analyses identified the revised multifocality criteria and the presence of two or more low-to-intermediate risk features as the major contributors to this reclassification (risk inflation). Conversely, refined compartment-based lymph node stratification was associated with improved classification accuracy. DCA demonstrated greater net clinical benefit for the 2025 system across clinically relevant threshold probabilities. CONCLUSIONS: The 2025 ATA initial risk stratification system significantly improves prognostic discrimination compared with the 2015 system. However, the enhanced sensitivity comes with a specificity trade-off, leading to substantial upward risk reclassification for recurrence-free patients. These real-world findings provide critical insights for clinicians to balance intensified surveillance against the potential for overtreatment under the new guidelines.

item.title: Effects of Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) in Cultured Human Vocal Fold Fibroblasts.
item.dc:creator: Kiessling P, Kimura A, Fauer A, Huang PY, Easwaran M, Erickson-DiRenzo E
item.description:
Authors: Kiessling P, Kimura A, Fauer A, Huang PY, Easwaran M, Erickson-DiRenzo E
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.70976
Published: 2026-Oct-07
PMID: 42844028



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Human exposures to fine particulate matter (PM2.5), a major air pollutant generated by multiple anthropogenic sources, are increasing worldwide. Though its adverse impacts on the lower airway are well-researched, PM2.5 has poorly understood effects on the upper airway. Our previous clinical research revealed increased dysphonia in the setting of elevated PM2.5 levels, though underlying interactions between PM2.5 and the vocal folds are unclear. This study evaluated the effects of PM2.5 on cultured human vocal fold fibroblasts (hVFFs), the primary cell type of the lamina propria. METHODS: Cultured hVFFs were exposed to increasing concentrations of PM2.5; unexposed cells served as control. After 24-72 h, cell morphology, cell viability, oxidative stress, and extracellular matrix and inflammatory gene expression were examined. Multivariate models estimated the association of PM2.5 concentration and cell viability. RESULTS: Morphologic analysis revealed persistent PM2.5 particles associated with hVFFs post-exposure, signifying extracellular adherence and/or intracellular migration. Increasing concentrations of PM2.5 induced elevated cytotoxicity and oxidative stress. Extracellular matrix and inflammatory gene expression were unaffected by exposure concentration or duration. CONCLUSION: Our findings provide an in vitro methodology for studying hVFF responses to PM2.5. In revealing the persistent cellular association of PM2.5 particles following exposures, as well as dose-dependent decreased cell viability and increased oxidative stress at higher PM2.5 concentrations, this work provides key initial insights into the effects of PM2.5 on hVFF. Findings from this work will provide a foundation for future in vitro and mechanistic studies of the cell-level effects of air pollution on the vocal folds. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

item.title: Storytelling in Medical Terminology: The Myths, Tales, and Pop Legends of Otolaryngology.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine the mythological, literary, folkloric, religious, and popular culture origins of eponymous terminology in otolaryngology and explore how these narrative associations continue to influence modern surgical education and clinical practice. DATA SOURCES: Published otolaryngology educational materials, historical texts, and peer-reviewed literature addressing eponymous anatomic landmarks, syndromes, radiographic findings, and reconstructive terminology associated with mythology, folklore, classic literature, religion, and cinema. REVIEW METHODS: A narrative historical review was performed using search terms including otolaryngology, eponym, mythology, classic literature, folklore, and legends. Terms were analyzed chronologically and thematically with attention to etymology, narrative origin, and present-day clinical relevance within otolaryngology and head and neck surgery. RESULTS: Numerous commonly used otolaryngologic terms derive from shared cultural narratives. Classical mythology informs terms such as the pterion, labyrinth, philtrum, Cupid's bow, and Lyre sign, linking anatomy and pathology to Greco-Roman mythic imagery. Religious and artistic traditions contribute terminology including Adam's apple and cherubism. Folklore and legend underpin entities such as Crocodile Tears syndrome, Ondine's curse, witch's chin, and pixie ear deformity, while modern popular culture has shaped descriptors including Pickwickian syndrome, Orphan Annie eye nuclei, Andy Gump deformity, and Spock brow. CONCLUSIONS: These eponyms serve not only as historical artifacts but also as cognitive and visual heuristics that condense complex anatomy, phenotype, and pathophysiology into memorable narrative constructs. Preserving awareness of these cultural roots enhances surgical education by leveraging the proven mnemonic power of storytelling and reminds clinicians that the language of medicine remains inseparable from the broader human experience. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility of a video flexible laryngeal mask airway (VFLMA) for simultaneous ventilation and direct visual RLN monitoring during thyroid surgery. METHODS: This prospective single-arm study enrolled 104 consecutive patients undergoing thyroid surgery, in whom the VFLMA provided real-time glottic views after induction. Six patients (5.8%) required conversion to endotracheal intubation with only 2 (1.9%) occurring during surgery. item.title: Neoadjuvant niraparib monotherapy for unresectable, homologous recombination deficiency-positive, high-grade serous ovarian cancer (NANT): a multicentre, single-arm, phase 2 trial.

item.description:
Authors: Liu D, Peng Z, Zhang W, Feng C, Wang P, Li J, Wen Y, Shan W, Xia Y, Li H, et al.
Journal: The Lancet. Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/S1470-2045(26)00387-6
Published: 2026-Oct-07
PMID: 42843394



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking surgery is standard treatment for advanced ovarian cancer that is unlikely to achieve optimal cytoreduction. We aimed to evaluate a chemotherapy-free regimen of neoadjuvant niraparib monotherapy in homologous recombination deficiency (HRD)-positive disease initially unsuitable for primary debulking surgery. METHODS: This single-arm, phase 2 trial was conducted at six tertiary hospitals in China. Eligible patients were aged 18-75 years, had treatment-naïve, FIGO stage III-IV HRD-positive high-grade serous or endometrioid ovarian cancer, an ECOG performance status of 0-2, with a low likelihood of complete primary debulking surgery based on prespecified criteria. Patients received oral niraparib monotherapy for two 28-day cycles with an individualised starting dose of 200 mg or 300 mg. Protocol-permitted supportive care was provided as clinically indicated. Co-primary endpoints were investigator-assessed objective response rate in the response-evaluable population and R0 resection rate after interval debulking surgery in the operated population. Safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose of niraparib. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04507841), is closed to enrolment, and this report presents the primary analysis. FINDINGS: Between Jan 8, 2021, and Jul 18, 2023, 127 patients were screened, and 67 were enrolled into the study. All enrolled patients were female and self-identified as Han Chinese (median age 55 years [IQR 50-62]). At the data cutoff (Dec 29, 2025), median follow-up was 37·7 months (IQR 31·8-48·5). Among 48 response-evaluable patients, 30 achieved an objective response, with an objective response rate of 63% (95% CI 47-76). Among 40 operated patients, 32 achieved R0 resection, with an R0 resection rate of 80% (95% CI 64-91). The most common grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were thrombocytopenia in 32 (48%) of 67 patients, leukopenia in 13 (19%) patients, anaemia in 12 (18%) patients, and neutropenia in nine (13%) patients. Serious adverse events occurred in 19 (28%) patients. No treatment-related deaths occurred. item.title: Differential associations between treatment delay and survival across head and neck cancer subsites: a national hospital-based framework for risk-stratified prioritization.
item.dc:creator: Sasaki AT, Boe LA, Eagan A, Patel SG, Moyses RA, Kowalski LP, Matos LL
item.description:
Authors: Sasaki AT, Boe LA, Eagan A, Patel SG, Moyses RA, Kowalski LP, Matos LL
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108168
Published: 2026-Oct-07
PMID: 42843070



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Delays in time to treatment initiation (TTI) have been associated with inferior outcomes in head and neck cancer, yet prior studies have typically evaluated tumors collectively, assuming uniform time sensitivity across diseases. This study quantified subsite- and stage-specific associations between TTI and overall survival (OS) and derived groups of tumors with similar TTI-mortality associations. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Cancer Database (2010-2017), including adults with head and neck malignancies treated with curative intent. Multivariable Cox models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for OS across each subsite-stage combination. Tumors were clustered according to the TTI threshold at which mortality risk became significantly elevated. RESULTS: The cohort included 211,406 patients. Early-stage tongue, floor of the mouth and glottic tumors, along with advanced tonsil and base of tongue cancers, showed increased mortality when TTI exceeded 30 days, forming the most time-sensitive category. Other tumors showed increased mortality at 60 days or 90 days. Salivary gland, lip and most advanced cancers showed no significant increase in mortality until ≥120 days. OS trajectories varied across the derived groups, reflecting heterogeneous associations between treatment timing and survival. CONCLUSION: Treatment delay has heterogeneous associations with mortality across head and neck subsites and stages. This derived framework identifies four TTI-sensitivity groups based on the timing at which excess adjusted mortality was observed. These findings may inform risk-stratified prioritization when treatment capacity is constrained but should not be interpreted as evidence that intentional treatment delay is clinically safe.

item.title: Feeding a low-protein diet exacerbates the susceptibility to Citrobacter rodentium and dextran sulfate sodium-induced intestinal injury in mice.
item.dc:creator: Thind MK, Flanagan M, de Wit S, Glembocki A, Pan J, Cuinat C, Leung S, Shaima SN, Sghayare H, Usmani K, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Thind MK, Flanagan M, de Wit S, Glembocki A, Pan J, Cuinat C, Leung S, Shaima SN, Sghayare H, Usmani K, et al.
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0335322
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42842553



Abstract:
Globally, almost half of all early childhood deaths are linked to severe undernutrition, herein referred to as severe malnutrition. Mortality in severely malnourished children is often attributed to common infectious diseases, including enteric infections. It has been proposed that impaired intestinal barrier function contributes to mortality, but direct evidence is limited and thus there exists a need to develop improved preclinical models to test these and other mechanistic hypotheses. In this study, we aimed to describe differences in response to enteric inflammation and infection in the colon of malnourished mice compared to well-nourished littermates. C57Bl/6 male weanlings were fed isocaloric diets, either a low 1% protein diet (LPD) or a control 18% protein diet (CPD) for 2-weeks either in combination with oral administration of dextran sodium sulfate (DSS), or Citrobacter rodentium (C. rodentium). LPD-fed mice were more susceptible to DSS or C. rodentium as evidenced by increased clinical severity scores, and reaching their humane endpoints. LPD-fed mice also showed more signs of colonic dysfunction with reduced levels of tight junction proteins, higher colonic pathogen load, and increased systemic inflammation and bacterial spread. Taken together, these observations show that malnourished animals have increased susceptibility to intestinal dysfunction caused by either chemical exposure or infection. These novel preclinical models can be used to further elucidate the processes involved in enteric dysfunction in malnutrition and to test therapies to improve intestinal repair and outcomes.

item.title: Comparative safety of imeglimin versus sitagliptin in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes: A pharmacy-based retrospective cohort study.
item.dc:creator: Suzuki N, Ooba N, Nakajima R, Takabatake K, Saita M, Kawakami E, Kawana M, Watanabe D, Hashiba H
item.description:
Authors: Suzuki N, Ooba N, Nakajima R, Takabatake K, Saita M, Kawakami E, Kawana M, Watanabe D, Hashiba H
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0359960
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42842541



Abstract:
Clinical evidence supports the safety and efficacy of imeglimin, a new oral antidiabetic medication that increases insulin secretion and reduces insulin resistance. However, comparative real-world safety data with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors, widely used in Japan, remain limited. This retrospective, pharmacy-based cohort study compared the incidence of adverse events (gastrointestinal events and hypoglycemia) among patients newly prescribed imeglimin or sitagliptin in real-world settings. Using a new-user design, we analyzed the 2022-2024 community pharmacy data across Japan, including 1,140 and 990 new imeglimin and sitagliptin users, respectively. Primary outcome (incidence of treatment-related events classified using Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities terminology) was evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models. Unadjusted and multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) for events during a 4-month follow-up were estimated. At least one adverse event was reported among 31% of imeglimin users versus 22% of sitagliptin users. Hypoglycemia risk differed non-significantly between groups (aHR: 0.66; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.20-2.22). However, imeglimin was associated with substantially higher risks of gastrointestinal events than sitagliptin (aHR: 5.44; 95% CI: 3.44-8.61), particularly nausea (aHR: 15.34; 95% CI: 3.50-67.23), diarrhea (aHR: 7.90; 95% CI: 2.54-24.62), and abdominal discomfort (aHR: 6.02; 95% CI: 1.47-24.58). Conversely, no significant difference was observed in hypoglycemia risk, although this finding should be interpreted with caution owing to the limited number of events. Involving community pharmacists allowed for active monitoring and identification of events that are often underreported in large-scale claims databases. Clinicians should prioritize gastrointestinal monitoring during initial stages of imeglimin therapy, particularly in older patients with complex treatment regimens.

item.title: Clinical and lifetime natural history of oral cancer: implications for screening and surveillance.
item.dc:creator: Cheung LC, Chen G, Muwonge R, Reeve M, Thomas G, Somanathan T, Mao F, Pan Q, Basu P, Sankaranarayanan R, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Cheung LC, Chen G, Muwonge R, Reeve M, Thomas G, Somanathan T, Mao F, Pan Q, Basu P, Sankaranarayanan R, et al.
Journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute | DOI: 10.1093/jnci/djag360
Published: 2026-Oct-07
PMID: 42842394



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: We estimated the clinical and lifetime natural history of oral cancer to inform empirical screening and surveillance algorithms. METHODS: We used data from ever-chewers/smokers/alcohol drinkers in the screening arm of the Kerala Oral Cancer Screening Trial (1996-2010), who attended at least one screen (n = 41,225) or two consecutive screens (n = 28,821). The clinical natural history (sensitivity, positive predictive value [PPV] and complement of negative predictive value [cNPV]) was estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods. The multistate natural history across initiation of chewing/smoking/drinking, precancer, early-stage cancer, late-stage cancer, and competing mortality was estimated using semi-Markov models. RESULTS: Visual-inspection over 2 consecutive screens (median=3.5 years apart [IQR=2.9-3.9]) had sensitivity=89.2%, PPV=1.55%, and NPV=99.96% for prevalent oral cancers (n = 83). On the first screen, 10.0% were positive with a referable oral lesion/precancer, and 12.9% were positive on either screen. Screen-positivity on both screens provided 32-fold risk-stratification for incident cancers over 11 years of follow-up (PPV=4.13% vs. cNPV in persistent screen-negatives=0.13%). Screen-positives on either screen accounted for 66.1% of incident oral cancers through 11 years of follow-up. In the lifetime/multistate model, an estimated mean=18.2% of ever-smokers/chewers/drinkers would develop oral precancer and mean=6.04% would progress from precancer to early-stage cancer (mean sojourn=19.3 years). The estimated mean sojourn time from early-stage to late-stage oral cancer was 2.7 years. CONCLUSIONS: Oral cancer screening intervals could be extended to 10 years for repeat negatives on 2 consecutive screens. The high PPV and short sojourn time from early-stage to late-stage cancer indicate the need for intensive surveillance among screen-positives with precancer. item.title: Impact of Neighborhood Socioeconomic Status on Presentation and Treatment of Thyroid Cancer.
item.dc:creator: Kandahari N, DeRouen MC, Li S, Hackman TG, Colaianni CA, Randolph GW, Russell MD
item.description:
Authors: Kandahari N, DeRouen MC, Li S, Hackman TG, Colaianni CA, Randolph GW, Russell MD
Journal: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery | DOI: 10.1002/ohn.70446
Published: 2026-Oct-07
PMID: 42841530



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We examined associations between multilevel sociodemographic factors and extent of disease at presentation and time to treatment in patients with differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC). STUDY DESIGN: Population-based study. SETTING: California Cancer Registry (CCR). METHODS: All adults diagnosed with DTC in California from January 1, 1988 to December 31, 2020 were included. Main independent variables were neighborhood socioeconomic status (nSES) and race/ethnicity. Covariates included individual sex, marital status, insurance type, and year and age at diagnosis. Primary outcomes were tumor histology, size, and stage at diagnosis. Secondary outcome was time from diagnosis to treatment. RESULTS: Among 88,894 individuals diagnosed with DTC, 77% were female, more were residents of higher SES neighborhoods (24% Q5 vs 13% Q1), and nearly half (48%) were non-Hispanic (NH) White, followed by 27% Hispanic and 7% of another NH Asian American ethnicity. In multivariable models, the odds of presenting with distant metastases were higher with lower nSES (OR Q1 vs Q5 = 1.33; 95% CI = 1.17, 1.50), male sex (OR female vs male = 0.43; 95% CI = 0.40, 0.47), and Black (OR = 1.24; 95% CI = 1.04, 1.49), Hispanic (OR = 2.02; 95% CI = 1.84, 2.21), Chinese American (OR = 1.80; 95% CI = 1.50, 2.16), Filipino American (OR = 2.07; 95% CI = 1.81, 2.36), or another Asian American (OR = 1.78; 95% CI = 1.56, 2.04) race/ethnicity. CONCLUSIONS: People of lower nSES, male sex, and certain racial/ethnic groups were diagnosed with more advanced disease and had longer times to receipt of definitive treatment. item.title: Reconstruction of Total Laryngectomy Defect Using Parascapular Free Flap: Case Series.

Authors: Al-Qurayshi Z, Molotkova E, Pipkorn P
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70502
Published: 2026-Oct-06
PMID: 42839736



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Reconstruction of total laryngectomy defects with vascularized tissue helps minimize the risk of pharyngocutaneous fistula development. Few studies have assessed outcomes following reconstruction with a parascapular free flap. METHODS: We identified 28 patients who underwent laryngectomy with parascapular free flap reconstruction between 2020 and 2024. Chart review was directed toward operative characteristics and postoperative outcomes, which were summarized using descriptive statistics. RESULTS: Thirteen out of 28 patients (46%) underwent salvage laryngectomy. Average operative time was 6.6 (±1.2) hours. Donor site morbidity was low; one patient experienced delayed wound dehiscence that was managed conservatively. Six patients developed pharyngocutaneous fistula; one patient required surgical intervention. The length of hospital stay ranged from 5 to 22 days, and the duration of postoperative nil per os status ranged from 7 to 56 days. CONCLUSIONS: Our experience demonstrates that the parascapular free flap is a viable option for reconstruction of defects secondary to laryngectomy.

item.title: Stability of GLOBOCAN Estimates Across Consecutive Releases: A Quantitative Benchmark for Global Cancer Epidemiology.
item.dc:creator: Sabuncuoğlu MZ, Zihni İ, Turan B, Acar S, Karaca İ
item.description:
Authors: Sabuncuoğlu MZ, Zihni İ, Turan B, Acar S, Karaca İ
Journal: International journal of cancer | DOI: 10.1002/ijc.70773
Published: 2026-Oct-06
PMID: 42839643



Abstract:
GLOBOCAN is the most widely used source of national cancer statistics, yet users routinely treat the difference between two releases as real epidemiological change. We quantified how far estimates move between the 2022 and 2024 cycles and whether this depends on development level. Age-standardised incidence and mortality rates for eight cancers were paired between GLOBOCAN 2022 and 2024 for 185 countries common to both cycles. Agreement was assessed by Bland-Altman analysis and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC); per-country revision magnitude was related to the Human Development Index (HDI) using rank and robust regression, with partial correlation adjusting for baseline incidence. Pooled concordance was high (CCC 0.97 for incidence, 0.95 for mortality) with negligible mean bias, but limits of agreement were wide and the tail heavy: 62.4%, 40.3%, 28.1% and 13.4% of country-cancer-sex cells were revised by more than 10%, 20%, 30% and 50%. Revision magnitude was inversely related to HDI (Spearman ρ = -0.62 for incidence and -0.62 for mortality; both p < 0.001), falling from 23.3% in low-HDI to 8.1% in very-high-HDI countries and persisted after adjustment for baseline incidence (partial ρ = -0.36); the development gradient is thus only partly explained by lower, more volatile baseline rates. Thyroid cancer showed the largest revisions. These findings provide, to our knowledge, the first quantitative benchmark for interpreting apparent differences between successive GLOBOCAN releases and support more cautious interpretation of single-cycle estimates from lower-HDI settings.

item.title: Salivary Microbiome Profiles in Burning Mouth Syndrome With Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease Comorbidity: A Comparative Analysis.

item.description:
Authors: Li L, Wu S, Cui Y, Wang L, Zhang X, Yan Z
Journal: Oral diseases | DOI: 10.1111/odi.70526
Published: 2026-Oct-06
PMID: 42839368



Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) has been recognized as a common comorbidity of burning mouth syndrome (BMS), suggesting potential interactions within the oral-gastrointestinal axis. This study aimed to test whether GERD comorbidity is associated with salivary microbiome profiles among patients with BMS. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Saliva samples from primary BMS patients without GERD (PBMS), BMS patients with GERD (GBMS), and healthy controls were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Microbial diversity, community structure, and differential taxa were assessed, and taxa were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis. RESULTS: Significant differences in salivary microbiome profiles were observed among GBMS, PBMS, and controls (p = 0.009). Both GBMS and PBMS showed higher abundances of Actinobacteriota and Rothia compared with controls, indicating shared BMS-associated microbial features. However, GBMS exhibited reduced microbial richness and enrichment of Porphyromonas and Parvimonas. CONCLUSIONS: BMS patients exhibit shared oral microbiome alterations, while GERD comorbidity is associated with a distinct salivary microbial profile characterized by reduced microbial richness and enrichment of Porphyromonas and Parvimonas. These findings suggest that GERD status may represent a potential clinical stratification factor for identifying biologically distinct subgroups of BMS, providing insight into disease heterogeneity and supporting future investigations of symptom variability and treatment response.

item.title: Outcomes and complications of parathyroidectomy in otorhinolaryngology practice: A single-institution, 10-year retrospective observational study.
item.dc:creator: Astl J, Rotnágl J, Holý R, Percik Y, Hložek J
item.description:
Authors: Astl J, Rotnágl J, Holý R, Percik Y, Hložek J
Journal: American journal of otolaryngology | DOI: 10.1016/j.amjoto.2026.104962
Published: 2026-Oct-03
PMID: 42849194



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Parathyroidectomy is associated with a spectrum of potential complications, including recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) injury, permanent hypocalcemia, postoperative hemorrhage, wound infection, and recurrence of hyperparathyroidism (HPT). The objective of this study was to evaluate the outcomes of 223 parathyroid procedures and to determine the incidence of procedure-related complications. METHODS: This retrospective observational study analyzed parathyroidectomy cases performed between 2013 and 2022. Demographic data and postoperative complications were collected and assessed. The success rates of surgical removal of parathyroid adenomas, hyperplasia, carcinomas, and cysts were evaluated in relation to preoperative and perioperative diagnostic methods. RESULTS: A total of 223 parathyroidectomy procedures were performed. Unilateral permanent RLN palsy was observed in 0.91% of cases (95% CI, 0.11-3.21%). Bilateral permanent vocal cord palsy was not observed. A positive response to the parathyroidectomy was observed in 98.43% (95% CI, 96.1-99.72%). Temporary hypercalcemia developed in 13.26% (95% CI, 9.41-18.35%). Revision surgery for persistent HPT or recurrence of HPT was necessary in 16 cases. CONCLUSION: The combination of preoperative multimodal imaging and precise hyperparathyroidism diagnosis is essential for reducing the risk of unsuccessful localization in parathyroid surgery. Ultrasound and scintigraphy offers the most effective diagnostic method. Intraoperative neuromonitoring is recommended for revision surgeries.

item.title: Genomic Landscape and Clinical Actionability of Skin Adnexal Carcinomas.
item.dc:creator: Costa Filho VO, Noronha MM, Costa Passos PR, Holanda Lopes CD, Leite GGF, Maia DCC, de Souza Wanderley CW, Saibil SD, Saldanha EF
item.description:
Authors: Costa Filho VO, Noronha MM, Costa Passos PR, Holanda Lopes CD, Leite GGF, Maia DCC, de Souza Wanderley CW, Saibil SD, Saldanha EF
Journal: JCO precision oncology | DOI: 10.1200/PO-26-00300
Published: 2026-Oct-01
PMID: 42868338



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Skin adnexal carcinomas (SACs) are rare and heterogeneous tumors with no established systemic treatment options and poor long-term survival rates in the advanced disease setting. Here, we aimed to characterize the genomic landscape and clinically actionable alterations across SAC subtypes. METHODS: We analyzed next-generation sequencing data from SACs in the American Association for Cancer Research Project GENIE. Mutations, copy number alterations, and structural variants were annotated using OncoKB. Actionable alterations were defined as Level 1-2 alterations or tumor mutational burden (TMB) ≥10 mut/Mb. TMB was compared across subtypes and with melanoma, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), and basal cell carcinoma (BCC). RESULTS: A total of 224 SACs were analyzed (49% extramammary Paget disease [EMPD], 33% apocrine/eccrine, 17% sebaceous, 1% follicular). In EMPD, the most frequent actionable alterations were in PIK3CA (25.7%) and ERBB2 (22.9%). In sebaceous carcinoma, actionable alterations were mainly in KRAS (10.3%) and PIK3CA (10.3%). Apocrine/eccrine tumors also presented ERBB2 and PIK3CA alterations, but at lower frequencies (5.5% and 8.2%, respectively). TMB-high occurred in 10.1% of EMPD, 28.2% of sebaceous, and 21.9% of apocrine/eccrine tumors, lower than in melanoma (52.1%), CSCC (64.4%), and BCC (63.3%). SAC drivers showed important heterogeneity across subtypes. Overall, 48.2% of SACs harbored at least one potentially actionable alteration. CONCLUSION: SACs frequently harbor clinically actionable alterations in a histotype-dependent manner. The identification of lineage-specific genomic differences underscores the clinical and translational relevance of integrating histology with genomic profiling for guiding therapeutic decision making.

item.title: Development of an MRI-based surgical difficulty scoring system for anterior and deep lobe parotid tumors.
item.dc:creator: Kim JH
item.description:
Authors: Kim JH
Journal: American journal of otolaryngology | DOI: 10.1016/j.amjoto.2026.104947
Published: 2026-Oct-01
PMID: 42863276



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Anterior and deep lobe parotid tumors present substantial technical challenges because of their close relationship to the facial nerve and deep parotid anatomy. We aimed to develop and internally validate a practical MRI-based scoring system to preoperatively predict surgical difficulty in these tumors. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent parotidectomy for anterior or deep lobe tumors between March 2020 and December 2024. A five-domain MRI-based difficulty score (range, 3-15) was constructed based on tumor location, size, relationship to the facial nerve, fat-plane integrity, and multifocality. Surgical difficulty was defined as prolonged operative time exceeding the 75th percentile. Predictive validity was assessed using operative time, estimated blood loss, and postoperative facial nerve outcomes. Interobserver reliability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analysis. Internal validation was performed in a standardized single-surgeon cohort. RESULTS: A total of 149 patients were included. Higher MRI-based difficulty scores were significantly associated with longer operative time and increased estimated blood loss (both p < 0.001). Postoperative facial nerve weakness occurred more frequently with increasing difficulty tiers (p = 0.01). These findings remained consistent in the standardized validation cohort (n = 36). Interobserver reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.87; 95% CI, 0.82-0.91), with minimal mean bias and narrow limits of agreement. CONCLUSIONS: This MRI-based difficulty score reliably predicts surgical complexity in anterior and deep lobe parotid tumors and demonstrates excellent interobserver reproducibility. It may serve as a useful preoperative tool for operative planning and risk stratification. External validation is warranted.

item.title: Executive Summary of the Clinical Practice Guideline on Tinnitus Update.
item.dc:creator: Adams ME, Cramer JD, Tunkel DE, Lee VS, Bourgeois JA, Eshraghi AA, Fagelson MA, White KB, Juliano AF, Kim H, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Adams ME, Cramer JD, Tunkel DE, Lee VS, Bourgeois JA, Eshraghi AA, Fagelson MA, White KB, Juliano AF, Kim H, et al.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Tinnitus is the perception of sound without an external source. More than 50 million people in the United States have reported experiencing tinnitus, resulting in an estimated prevalence of 10% to 15% in adults. The focus of this guideline is on tinnitus that is both bothersome and persistent (lasting 6 months or longer), which often negatively affects the patient's quality of life. The target audience for the guideline is any clinician, including allied health professionals, involved in managing patients with tinnitus. The target patient population is limited to adults (18 years and older) with tinnitus that is persistent and bothersome. PURPOSE: The purpose of this guideline is to provide and update evidence-based recommendations for clinicians managing patients with tinnitus. The target audience for this guideline is any clinician involved in managing patients with tinnitus. People with tinnitus may be evaluated by a variety of health care providers, including primary care clinicians, specialty clinicians, and allied health professionals including audiologists and clinical psychologists. The target patient population is limited to adults (18 years and older) with tinnitus that is persistent and bothersome. Most people with tinnitus have associated hearing loss, such as sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) secondary to aging (presbycusis), noise exposure (noise-induced hearing loss), or acoustic trauma. Tinnitus can also be a symptom of numerous auditory and non-auditory system disorders, ranging from middle ear diseases, such as otosclerosis and eustachian tube dysfunction, to inner ear and auditory nerve pathologies such as Ménière's disease and vestibular schwannoma. Nonauditory system disorders that can cause tinnitus include vascular anomalies, myoclonus, and intracranial hypertension. The Guideline Update Group (GUG) placed emphasis on the need for thorough clinical evaluation to identify these potentially treatable and sometimes serious disorders. However, patients with identifiable causative diagnoses other than sensorineural hearing loss are excluded from this guideline as they are excluded from nearly all randomized controlled trials of tinnitus management, making it impossible to generalize trial results to these patients. Nevertheless, clinicians should decide whether to apply the recommendations of this guideline to patients with these conditions on an individualized basis. The guideline also underscores the need to distinguish between subjective, objective, and pulsatile tinnitus to further direct patient evaluation and management. Comprehensive management of objective tinnitus and pulsatile tinnitus is not within the scope of this guideline. Pulsatile tinnitus is the perception of a rhythmic sound in the absence of an external source that may be pulse-synchronous, which is often but not always related to vascular causes, or pulse-asynchronous, which is typically associated with mechanical causes such as palatal or middle ear myoclonus.1 Further, the guideline does not apply to transient ear noise, which is the sudden perception of a tonal or ringing sound in 1 ear, lasting fewer than 5 minutes, that may be accompanied by a sense of hearing loss or aural fullness, as it does not typically require clinical management.2 The guideline also excludes patients with tinnitus related to complex auditory hallucinations or hallucinations related to psychotic or seizure disorders. This is an update to an evidence-based clinical guideline developed for the evaluation and management of tinnitus. This updated guideline provides clinicians with a logical framework to improve patient care and mitigate the personal and social effects of persistent, bothersome tinnitus. The first part of the guideline is focused on the clinical evaluation of patients with tinnitus, including the history, physical exam, and selection and timing of diagnostic testing and specialty referral to identify potential underlying treatable pathology and reduce the risk of self-harm. The remainder of the guideline is focused on the evaluation and treatment of patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus, with recommendations to evaluate and measure its effects as well as to determine the most appropriate interventions to improve symptoms and quality of life. ACTION STATEMENTS: The Guideline Update Group made strong recommendations for the following Key Action Statements (KAS): Clinicians should distinguish patients with bothersome tinnitus from patients with nonbothersome tinnitus (KAS 2). Clinicians should inquire about risks for self-harm in a patient with bothersome tinnitus (KAS 3). Clinicians should not obtain neuroradiologic imaging in patients with tinnitus specifically to evaluate the tinnitus unless specific concerning features are present (KAS 6). The Guideline Update Group made recommendations for the following KASs: Clinicians should perform a targeted history and physical examination at the initial evaluation of a patient with tinnitus (KAS 1). Clinicians should obtain a comprehensive audiological evaluation in patients with tinnitus (KAS 5). Clinicians should educate patients with tinnitus about the natural history and effects of, and management strategies for tinnitus (KAS 7). Clinicians should recommend a hearing aid evaluation for patients with hearing difficulties and persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 8). Clinicians should refer patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus for cochlear implant evaluation when they meet audiologic criteria for referral (KAS 9). Clinicians should recommend Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 11). Clinicians or their designee should assess and document outcomes of interventions in patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 15). The Guideline Update Group made recommendations against for the following KASs: Clinicians should not routinely recommend antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, or intratympanic medications for a primary indication of treating persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 12). Clinicians should not recommend dietary supplements for the primary indication of persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 13). Clinicians should not recommend repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for the treatment of patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 14A). The Guideline Update Group offered options for the following KASs: Clinicians may inquire about somatosensory features in patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 4). Clinicians may recommend sound enrichment to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 10). Clinicians may offer bimodal neuromodulation to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 14B).

item.title: Roxadustat Treatment After PCI Among Patients With ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.dc:creator: Quan W, Wang Y, Zhang M, Zhu T, Zhu J, Wang X, Zhu Z, Du R, Ding F, Ni J, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Quan W, Wang Y, Zhang M, Zhu T, Zhu J, Wang X, Zhu Z, Du R, Ding F, Ni J, et al.
Journal: JAMA network open | DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.37953
Published: 2026-Oct-01
PMID: 42853570



Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Preclinical studies suggest that stabilization of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) may attenuate reperfusion injury. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether oral roxadustat, a HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, reduced infarct size when administered after reperfusion among patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This phase 2, open-label, randomized clinical trial-Effect of Roxadustat in Acute Myocardial Infarction (ROXAMI)-enrolled adults with STEMI undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) at a single tertiary medical center between April 1, 2021, and March 31, 2024, with follow-up through 1 year. INTERVENTIONS: Oral roxadustat (100 mg, 3 times per week for 2 weeks), initiated within 2 hours after primary PCI, or standard care alone. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary end point was infarct size as a percentage of the left ventricle at 30 days measured by late gadolinium enhancement on [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Prespecified secondary end points included major adverse cardiovascular events, myocardial injury markers, echocardiographic parameters, and myocardial fibroblast activation parameters on [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET and MRI. The primary efficacy analysis for infarct size was conducted in the modified intention-to-treat population. RESULTS: Among 158 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 63.6 [11.0] years; 133 men [84.2%]; 79 randomized to each group), 148 (93.7%; 72 roxadustat and 76 control) had evaluable imaging for the primary outcome. For the primary end point, mean (SD) infarct size did not significantly differ between the roxadustat and control groups (23.3% [12.2%] vs 22.0% [12.2%]; mean difference, 1.3 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.7 to 5.3 percentage points; P = .51). Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 3 of 79 patients (3.8%) in the roxadustat group and 7 of 79 (8.9%) in the control group (hazard ratio, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.11-1.63; P = .21). In multiplicity-unadjusted secondary analyses, adjusted between-group differences at 12 months were 2.9 percentage points (95% CI, 0.4-5.3 percentage points; P = .02) for the change in left ventricular ejection fraction (mean [SD]: roxadustat, 3.4% [0.9%] vs control, 0.5% [0.9%]) and -4.5 mL/m2 (95% CI, -8.9 to -0.1 mL/m2; P = .045) for left ventricular end-diastolic volume index (mean [SD]: roxadustat, 1.2 [1.6] mL/m2 vs control, 5.7 [1.6] mL/m2). The incidence of prespecified safety end points did not differ between the roxadustat and control groups. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial of patients with STEMI, roxadustat administration after PCI did not significantly reduce infarct size at 30 days compared with control. Secondary ventricular remodeling findings were exploratory and require confirmation. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04803864.

item.title: Bridging Clinical Observational Research and Data Standards in Head and Neck Cancer Care: Scoping Review and Mapping of Clinical Data Elements.

item.description:
Authors: Valerie IC, Aly F, Niknam Shirvan G, Alam FI, Johnston M, Kong BY, Findlay M, Holloway L, Kennedy G
Journal: JCO clinical cancer informatics | DOI: 10.1200/CCI-26-00177
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42848982



Abstract:
PURPOSE: A scoping review and mapping of clinical data elements in observational studies were conducted to assess head and neck cancer (HNC) clinical data, alignment with existing observational oncology data standards, and the demonstrated opportunities for using these data standards in observational studies. METHODS: The scoping review was performed to systematically find and extract data elements from real-world studies emphasizing HNC treatment patterns. Text-embedding-assisted and manual mapping was performed to map data elements to their representations in HNC Ontology, Operational Ontology for Oncology, Minimal Common Oncology Data Elements, and the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model. Study characteristics, data elements and their mapping, and proportion of clinical domains represented were analyzed. Demonstrated opportunities for using standard data elements were reviewed based on the mapping results. RESULTS: A total of 98 observational studies were included. National databases were the most common data source (59.2%), and disease trajectory outcomes were the most frequently reported study end point (95.9%). Overall, 1,613 data elements were reported and classified into five domains: diagnosis (1.2%), health system (5.7%), tumor (27.2%), person (32.7%), and treatment (33.2%). Mapping coverage varied across domains, with 85%-100% coverage in diagnosis, 83.6%-95.2% in treatment, 85.3%-97.8% in tumor, 50.7%-89% in person, and 43.8%-81.2% in health system domains. Demonstrated opportunities for applying data standardization include facilitating geographical links to personal data elements, streamlining value derivation of longitudinally tracked data elements, and deriving complex treatment constructs. CONCLUSION: The existing data standards and associated terminology systems covered most of the clinical observational data elements, but gaps remain in structuring complex treatment factors that may affect patient outcomes. Resulting mapping offers generalizable representations across standards, laying the groundwork for further refinement through collaborative data element curation from local conventions under the guidance of data standard experts.
